# Technical Drawing — voice recording scripts

<!-- GENERATED by scripts/build_drawing_scripts.mts — edit the lesson, not this file. -->

The lessons are the source of truth. Each `####` heading below is **one MP3** — copy its whole block and feed it
to your voice generator in one go. One clip is one step of the lesson, and the step ends when the clip ends, so a
clip is never split into several files.

## How to record and wire the voices in

1. Copy a block, generate the voice, and save it at the path in its heading, under `public/sounds/technical-drawing/`.
   So the first block below is saved as `public/sounds/technical-drawing/blend-arcs/what-is-a-blend.mp3`.
2. Leave the `[pause]` markers in. They are where the on-screen caption changes line, and the caption generator
   finds those silences in the finished MP3 with ffmpeg to line the words up with the voice.
   Aim for about half a second of silence at each one.
3. Run `node scripts/generate_narration_captions.mjs scripts/narration/technical-drawing.captions.json`.
   That measures every MP3 it can find and rewrites `src/lib/audio/narration/technicalDrawing.ts`.
4. That is all. The step retimes itself to the clip: the captions, the pointing hand and the pencil all follow the
   recorded voice, so a re-recorded take needs no code change.

A step whose clip has not been recorded yet falls back to estimated timings and runs silently, so a half-recorded
topic still plays end to end.

### Do not edit this file

It is generated from the lessons. To change what is said, change the topic in
`src/features/practicals/polytechnic/technical-drawing/topicsConstructions.ts` and run:

```bash
npx tsx scripts/build_drawing_scripts.mts
```

That rewrites this file and the captions script together, so the words the narrator reads can never drift from the
words the app shows. If they drift, the generator spreads the script across the wrong speech and the captions slide
out of time for the rest of the clip.

### Voice

Tinashe, the same instructor as the science practicals: unhurried, warm, speaking to somebody meeting a drawing
board for the first time. Short sentences. Read the numbers as words — "one hundred and forty", not "140".

## Straight lines joined to curves by an arc

_Topic id `blend-arcs` · 5 steps · folder `public/sounds/technical-drawing/blend-arcs/`_

#### `blend-arcs/what-is-a-blend.mp3` — A corner that flows

```text
Real parts do not have sharp corners. They have rounded ones. [pause]
A rounded corner is stronger, and it is safer to handle. [pause]
On a drawing we call it a blend, or a fillet, or just a radius. [pause]
The arc must flow into the straight line with no kink at all. [pause]
The place where they meet is called the tangent point. [pause]
Get the tangent points right and the drawing looks professional. Get them wrong and it looks broken.
```

#### `blend-arcs/right-angle-lines.mp3` — The two lines to be joined

```text
Start with the easiest case. Two lines meeting at a right angle. [pause]
Draw them a little longer than you need. [pause]
The extra will be rubbed out at the end, once we know where the arc lands. [pause]
The question says join these with a radius of forty.
```

#### `blend-arcs/right-angle-blend.mp3` — Find the centre 40 from both lines

```text
Here is the rule for every blend on this sheet. [pause]
The centre of the arc must be forty away from the first line, and forty away from the second. [pause]
So draw a light line forty from the upright one, running parallel to it. [pause]
And another forty from the horizontal one. [pause]
Where those two light lines cross is the centre. [pause]
Now drop back to each line at ninety degrees. Those are your tangent points. [pause]
Needle on the centre, and swing from one tangent point to the other. [pause]
Then rub out the corner. The arc is the corner now.
```

#### `blend-arcs/acute-blend.mp3` — The same rule on a sharp corner

```text
Now a corner that is not a right angle. Sixty degrees this time. [pause]
Do not panic. The rule has not changed at all. [pause]
Draw a light line thirty away from each arm, parallel to it. [pause]
Where they cross is the centre. [pause]
Perpendicular back to each arm gives the tangent points. [pause]
And swing the arc between them. [pause]
Notice the tangent points are not the same distance from the corner as before. [pause]
That is normal. Never guess them. Always construct them.
```

#### `blend-arcs/line-to-circle.mp3` — Joining a straight line to a curve

```text
Last case, and this is the one the exam likes. [pause]
A straight line, a circle, and an arc joining them. [pause]
The line part has not changed. The centre must be forty from the line. [pause]
Now the circle. The circle has a radius of thirty-two. [pause]
Our blend is forty. So the centre must be thirty-two plus forty from the circle centre. [pause]
That is seventy-two. Add them together. [pause]
So swing an arc of seventy-two from the circle centre, and see where it meets the parallel line. [pause]
And here is the last piece. The tangent point on the circle is on the line joining the two centres. [pause]
That is always true when two curves touch. Join the centres, and you cross at the touching point.
```

## An ellipse and scales

_Topic id `ellipse-and-scales` · 7 steps · folder `public/sounds/technical-drawing/ellipse-and-scales/`_

#### `ellipse-and-scales/what-is-an-ellipse.mp3` — A circle seen from an angle

```text
An ellipse is a squashed circle. [pause]
You see one every day. Look at a cup from an angle. The round top looks like an ellipse. [pause]
Any circle drawn on a sloping face becomes an ellipse on your paper. [pause]
It has two axes. The long way across is the major axis. [pause]
The short way is the minor axis. [pause]
They cross in the middle, at ninety degrees. [pause]
Ours is one hundred and sixty long, and one hundred wide.
```

#### `ellipse-and-scales/two-circles.mp3` — Draw the two circles

```text
Now draw two circles, both on the same centre. [pause]
The big one has the major axis as its diameter. So the radius is eighty. [pause]
The small one has the minor axis as its diameter. Radius fifty. [pause]
Remember, the question gives you the full width, and the compass wants half of it. [pause]
These two circles do all the work for us.
```

#### `ellipse-and-scales/radial-lines.mp3` — Draw radial lines every 30°

```text
Now draw lines out from the centre, straight through both circles. [pause]
Every thirty degrees. Your thirty sixty set square gives you all of them. [pause]
Twelve lines in total. [pause]
If you want a smoother curve, draw more. Every fifteen degrees is better. [pause]
Each line cuts the big circle in one place, and the small circle in another.
```

#### `ellipse-and-scales/plot-points.mp3` — Across from one circle, down from the other

```text
Here is the clever part. Take one radial line at a time. [pause]
From where it cuts the big circle, drop a line straight down. [pause]
From where it cuts the small circle, draw a line straight across. [pause]
Where those two meet is a point on the ellipse. [pause]
Down from the big one. Across from the small one. Do not mix them up. [pause]
Now do that for all twelve lines. [pause]
Twelve points appear, and you can already see the shape.
```

#### `ellipse-and-scales/join-curve.mp3` — Join the points with a French curve

```text
Now join the points into a smooth curve. [pause]
Do not use a compass. An ellipse is not made of arcs, and it has no one centre. [pause]
Use a French curve. Line it up on three or four points at a time. [pause]
Draw a little, slide along, and match it to the next points. [pause]
Always overlap what you have drawn, or you will leave a kink. [pause]
Take your time here. This is the part the examiner looks at.
```

#### `ellipse-and-scales/plain-scale.mp3` — Now a plain scale

```text
Second half of the lesson. Scales. [pause]
A drawing at one to fifty means everything is fifty times smaller than real life. [pause]
You could divide every measurement by fifty. That is slow and you will make mistakes. [pause]
So instead we draw a ruler for this one drawing. That is a plain scale. [pause]
We want to read up to five metres. [pause]
Five metres divided by fifty is one hundred millimetres. So the scale is one hundred long. [pause]
Draw a thin box, one hundred by ten. [pause]
Then divide it into five equal parts. Each part is one whole metre.
```

#### `ellipse-and-scales/subdivide-scale.mp3` — Subdivide the first division

```text
Now the part everybody gets wrong. Where do we write zero? [pause]
Not at the left end. Zero goes at the start of the second division. [pause]
Everything to the right of zero counts whole metres. One, two, three, four. [pause]
And that first division, on the left of zero, gets cut into ten small parts. [pause]
Each small part is one tenth of a metre. That is a decimetre. [pause]
So to measure three point four metres, you put one leg on the three, [pause]
and the other leg four small parts to the left of zero. [pause]
Whole units to the right, tenths to the left. Write that down. [pause]
Always letter what the scale reads, and always write the ratio underneath.
```

## First angle orthographic projection

_Topic id `orthographic` · 9 steps · folder `public/sounds/technical-drawing/orthographic/`_

#### `orthographic/read-the-block.mp3` — Look at the block first

```text
Here is a solid block. Look at it carefully before you draw anything. [pause]
It is like a step. A tall part on the left, and a low part on the right. [pause]
It is eighty long, fifty deep, and sixty high. [pause]
Now, paper is flat. The block is not flat. So we cannot draw it as it is. [pause]
Instead we look at it from three directions, and draw what we see each time. [pause]
Look from the front. That gives the front view, or the elevation. [pause]
Look from on top, straight down. That gives the plan. [pause]
Look from the side. That gives the end view. [pause]
Three flat pictures. Together they describe the whole solid, with no guessing.
```

#### `orthographic/set-out.mp3` — Set out where the views go

```text
Before drawing, we decide where each view will sit. This is called setting out. [pause]
Beginners skip this, then run out of paper. Do not skip it. [pause]
The front view goes here, at the top left. [pause]
Now listen, because this is the rule of first angle. [pause]
In first angle, the view you get by looking from the top is drawn underneath. [pause]
And the view you get by looking from the left is drawn on the right. [pause]
It feels backwards at first. It is because the object is pushed away from you. [pause]
Leave about thirty millimetres of space between the views, so the drawing can breathe. [pause]
Draw these boxes very lightly with your 2H. They are only guides.
```

#### `orthographic/front-view.mp3` — Draw the front view

```text
We always start with the view that shows the most shape. [pause]
Here that is the front view. Looking from the front, the block looks like a letter L. [pause]
Start at the bottom left corner and go across. Eighty millimetres. [pause]
Now up the right side. Only thirty, because that side is the low part. [pause]
Now across to the left, forty. This is the top of the step. [pause]
Now up again, thirty more, to reach sixty. [pause]
Now across the top, forty, and finally down the left side. [pause]
And you are back where you started. That shape is the front view.
```

#### `orthographic/project-down.mp3` — Project down to the plan

```text
Now the plan. And here is the part that saves you time. [pause]
You do not measure the plan again. You bring the sizes down from the front view. [pause]
Take your set square and drop a light line straight down from every corner. [pause]
Down from the left edge. [pause]
Down from the step. [pause]
And down from the right edge. [pause]
These light lines are called projectors. They carry the width downwards. [pause]
The width of the plan is now fixed. It must match the front view exactly. [pause]
That is the whole idea of projection. The views line up.
```

#### `orthographic/draw-plan.mp3` — Complete the plan

```text
Now measure the one size the front view cannot give you. The depth. [pause]
The depth is fifty millimetres. [pause]
Draw the top line and the bottom line of the plan with your T-square. [pause]
Close the two ends on your projectors. [pause]
Now one more line. Where the step falls, there is an edge you can see from above. [pause]
So draw a full line there, not a dashed one. You can see it, so it is solid. [pause]
Your plan is a rectangle, eighty by fifty, with one line across it.
```

#### `orthographic/mitre-line.mp3` — Draw the 45° mitre line

```text
Now we need the end view, on the right. [pause]
The heights come across from the front view. That is easy, they are level. [pause]
But the depth is in the plan, and the plan is below. The depth is going the wrong way. [pause]
So we use a clever line. The mitre line. [pause]
Take your forty-five degree set square and draw a line at forty-five degrees. [pause]
It starts level with the top of the plan, and under the left of the end view. [pause]
What does it do? It bends a measurement round a corner. [pause]
A depth measured going down becomes the same depth measured going across. [pause]
That is all it is. A corner for measurements to turn on.
```

#### `orthographic/project-across.mp3` — Bring the sizes to the end view

```text
Now we feed the end view from two directions. [pause]
First, heights. Draw light lines straight across from the front view. [pause]
From the bottom, from the step at thirty, and from the top at sixty. [pause]
Second, depths. Draw light lines across from the plan until they touch the mitre line. [pause]
Where each one touches the mitre line, turn and go straight up. [pause]
Across, hit the mitre, turn up. Across, hit the mitre, turn up. [pause]
Those upward lines give you the front and the back of the end view.
```

#### `orthographic/end-view.mp3` — Complete the end view

```text
Now line in the end view, using the crossings you made. [pause]
It comes out as a plain rectangle. Fifty wide, and sixty high. [pause]
Why a plain rectangle? Because you are looking at the tall part, and it hides the step. [pause]
But wait. The step is still there. It is just behind. [pause]
And in technical drawing, we never pretend a feature is not there. [pause]
So we show it with a dashed line, level with the step, at thirty. [pause]
A dashed line means, this edge is there, but you cannot see it from here. [pause]
We call it hidden detail. Students forget it and lose easy marks. Do not forget it.
```

#### `orthographic/dimension-and-label.mp3` — Dimension and label the views

```text
Last part. We put the sizes on, and we name the views. [pause]
Dimension lines are thin, with arrowheads touching the projection lines. [pause]
The number sits on top of the line, in the middle, and you read it from the bottom or from the right. [pause]
Now a rule that catches everybody. [pause]
Each size is written once, in one view only. Never twice. [pause]
If you put eighty on the front view and eighty on the plan, that is a fault. [pause]
Now letter the name under each view. Front view. Plan. End view. [pause]
And finally, go over your outlines with the HB so they are black and strong. [pause]
Leave the light construction lines. Do not rub them out. They are your working. [pause]
That is a complete first angle drawing. Well done.
```

## Isometric drawing

_Topic id `isometric` · 7 steps · folder `public/sounds/technical-drawing/isometric/`_

#### `isometric/what-is-isometric.mp3` — What isometric means

```text
Last lesson we cut a block into three flat views. [pause]
Today we do the opposite. We draw the whole block as one picture. [pause]
This is called isometric drawing. [pause]
Isometric means equal measure. Iso is equal. Metric is measure. [pause]
It has three directions, and only three. [pause]
Height goes straight up. Always straight up, never slanted. [pause]
Length goes up to the right, at thirty degrees. [pause]
Depth goes up to the left, at thirty degrees. [pause]
Thirty degrees. That is exactly what your set square gives you, so you never guess.
```

#### `isometric/axes.mp3` — Draw the three axes

```text
Start with a dot. This will be the front bottom corner of the block. [pause]
It is the corner nearest to your eye. [pause]
From that dot, draw a line straight up. That is the height axis. [pause]
Now put the thirty sixty set square on your T-square. [pause]
Draw a line going up to the right at thirty degrees. That is the length axis. [pause]
Now turn the set square over and draw up to the left, also thirty degrees. [pause]
Three lines from one corner. That is your frame for everything else.
```

#### `isometric/mark-sizes.mp3` — Mark the real sizes on the axes

```text
Now the sizes. And this is the good news. [pause]
On these three lines, you measure the real size. No shrinking, no scaling. [pause]
Eighty long, so measure eighty along the right hand line. [pause]
Fifty deep, so measure fifty along the left hand line. [pause]
Sixty high, so measure sixty straight up. [pause]
One warning, and it is the biggest mistake in isometric. [pause]
You may only measure along these three directions. [pause]
Never put your rule on a slanting corner that is not one of the three. That length is false.
```

#### `isometric/crate.mp3` — Build the crate

```text
Now we build a box. We call it the crate. [pause]
Imagine a wooden box that the block fits into exactly, with no space left over. [pause]
Eighty by fifty by sixty. Draw it in light construction lines. [pause]
Every line is parallel to one of your three axes. There are no other directions. [pause]
So slide the set square along and keep drawing parallels. [pause]
It is a box in the air. Take your time and it will look solid. [pause]
This way of working is called the crating method. [pause]
You draw the box first, then you cut pieces off it. Like a carpenter.
```

#### `isometric/cut-step.mp3` — Cut the step out of the crate

```text
Now we cut the step. [pause]
The step starts forty millimetres along the length. [pause]
Mark that on the bottom front edge, and carry it up the crate. [pause]
The step is thirty millimetres high. [pause]
Mark thirty up the front corner, and carry it across. [pause]
Where those two meet, the piece above and to the right comes off. [pause]
Draw the two new faces you have just made. [pause]
One face standing up, and one face lying flat.
```

#### `isometric/line-in.mp3` — Line in the finished block

```text
Now line in. Take the HB and press a little harder. [pause]
Go over only the edges you can actually see. [pause]
Here is the difference from last lesson. [pause]
In orthographic we drew hidden edges as dashed lines. [pause]
In isometric we do not. We leave the hidden edges out completely. [pause]
There are three of them, and they all meet at the back bottom corner, hiding behind the block. [pause]
Your outline should now be dark and clear, standing above the light crate lines. [pause]
Look at it. It looks solid. That is why we draw isometric. [pause]
One drawing anybody can understand, even someone who cannot read a projection.
```

#### `isometric/finish-iso.mp3` — Tidy up and label

```text
Finally, tidy the sheet. [pause]
Clean off the loose graphite with a soft eraser or a brush. [pause]
Do not rub your construction lines away. They are light, and they belong there. [pause]
Never use your hand to sweep the sheet. Your hand leaves a grey smudge. [pause]
Letter the title under the drawing. [pause]
And fill in the title block in the corner if you have not already. [pause]
That is isometric drawing finished. [pause]
You now know how to set up a sheet, construct with a compass, and draw a solid two different ways. [pause]
Practise each one three times on real paper. The board teaches your hands, not just your head.
```

## Bars

_Topic id `bars` · 6 steps · folder `public/sounds/technical-drawing/bars/`_

#### `bars/why-break.mp3` — Why we break a bar

```text
Today we draw bars — round bar, square bar and hexagon bar. [pause]
A bar is long. Three metres of it will not fit on your sheet. [pause]
So we use a convention. We draw both ends, and break out the middle. [pause]
The break line says: the part carries on, I have just taken a piece out. [pause]
The dimension still says the true length. The drawing is short, the bar is not.
```

#### `bars/round-bar.mp3` — Round bar and its break

```text
Start with the round bar. Two lines along the T-square, thirty apart. [pause]
Close both ends with a short vertical line. [pause]
Now put in the centre line, thin and long-short-long. [pause]
Here comes the break. Freehand, not with the square. [pause]
It waves out one side, back through the middle, and out the other side. [pause]
That S is the sign for solid round material. Learn it — it is examined.
```

#### `bars/round-section.mp3` — Cut it and hatch it

```text
Beside it we show the section — what you see if you saw the bar through. [pause]
Swing a circle of the same diameter. [pause]
Now hatch it. Thin lines at forty-five degrees, evenly spaced. [pause]
Hatching must stop on the outline. Never let it run outside the metal. [pause]
Solid section, so the hatching goes right across. Nothing is hollow here.
```

#### `bars/square-bar.mp3` — Square bar, zigzag break

```text
Square bar next, thirty across the flats. [pause]
The break is different. Square and flat material takes a zigzag. [pause]
One sharp z in the middle of the line, drawn freehand. [pause]
The end view is a square, hatched the same forty-five degrees.
```

#### `bars/hex-bar.mp3` — Hexagon bar across flats

```text
Hexagon bar last. This is the material every nut and bolt head is made from. [pause]
In the side view it looks like square bar, so we letter it A slash F. [pause]
The end view is a true hexagon. Use the thirty-sixty set square. [pause]
Across the flats is thirty. Across the corners is bigger — thirty four point six. [pause]
The stores will ask you for across flats. Give them that, not the corners.
```

#### `bars/dimension-bars.mp3` — Dimension the true length

```text
Last job: the sizes. [pause]
Diameter thirty on the round bar. The symbol is a circle with a stroke through it. [pause]
Thirty across flats on the square and the hexagon. [pause]
And the length — two hundred and fifty — written across the break. [pause]
That is the convention working for you. Short drawing, true size.
```

## Tubes

_Topic id `tubes` · 5 steps · folder `public/sounds/technical-drawing/tubes/`_

#### `tubes/tube-vs-bar.mp3` — A tube is a bar with a hole

```text
A tube is a bar with a hole down the middle. [pause]
That hole is called the bore. [pause]
The metal left round it is the wall. [pause]
Outside diameter, take away the bore, divide by two. That is your wall thickness. [pause]
Forty outside, twenty-eight bore. Forty take twenty-eight is twelve, halved is six.
```

#### `tubes/tube-body.mp3` — Draw the tube

```text
Two outside lines, forty apart, along the T-square. [pause]
Inside them, two more for the bore. [pause]
The bore is inside the metal, so you cannot see it. Draw it hidden — short dashes. [pause]
Centre line down the middle, long-short-long. [pause]
Close the ends. Now it is a tube, not four lines.
```

#### `tubes/tube-break.mp3` — Break it open

```text
The break on a tube is not one wave. It is one on each wall. [pause]
Top wall waves through its own thickness. [pause]
Bottom wall does the same. [pause]
The gap in the middle is the bore, left open. [pause]
Anybody looking at this knows straight away: hollow, and that thick.
```

#### `tubes/tube-section.mp3` — Section the tube

```text
Two circles for the end view: outside diameter, then the bore. [pause]
Cut it through and you get a ring. [pause]
Hatch the ring. Do not hatch the hole. [pause]
Hatching in the bore is the commonest mistake in the whole paper.
```

#### `tubes/tube-dims.mp3` — Three sizes, no more

```text
Outside diameter forty. Bore twenty-eight. [pause]
Those two fix everything. The wall is already decided. [pause]
If you dimension all three you have over-dimensioned the drawing. [pause]
Over-dimensioning loses marks, because two workshops can then argue about which one to work to.
```

## Shafts##################################################################################
#########################################################################################

_Topic id `shafts` · 6 steps · folder `public/sounds/technical-drawing/shafts/`_

#### `shafts/shaft-job.mp3` — What a shaft has to do

```text
A shaft carries the drive. It turns, so it is round. [pause]
It is not one diameter all the way. It is stepped. [pause]
Each step is there for something: a bearing here, a gear there. [pause]
The face where one step meets the next is called a shoulder. [pause]
The shoulder is what stops the bearing sliding along. It locates it.
```

#### `shafts/shaft-centre.mp3` — Centre line first

```text
A round part starts with its centre line. Always. [pause]
Long, short, long. Thin. Running past both ends of the part. [pause]
Everything else is measured off this line, half a diameter each way.
```

#### `shafts/shaft-steps.mp3` — Step the diameters out

```text
Twelve above the line and twelve below gives you twenty-four diameter. [pause]
Then twenty each way for the forty bearing seat. [pause]
Then fifteen each way for the thirty on the output end. [pause]
Join the steps with vertical lines. Those are your shoulders. [pause]
Leave a gap along the top of the bearing seat. The keyway is cut there.
```

#### `shafts/shaft-chamfer.mp3` — Chamfer both ends

```text
Never leave a sharp corner on the end of a shaft. [pause]
Take a small chamfer with the forty-five set square. [pause]
Two by forty-five degrees is the usual one. [pause]
It saves fingers, and it helps the shaft start into the bearing.
```

#### `shafts/shaft-keyway.mp3` — Cut the keyway

```text
The gear must not spin on the shaft. So we key it. [pause]
A key is a rectangular block sitting half in the shaft, half in the gear. [pause]
The slot in the shaft is the keyway. [pause]
Draw it on the bearing seat, five deep, and let it break the outline. [pause]
And show the end view, so the width and the depth can both be seen.
```

#### `shafts/shaft-dims.mp3` — Dimension from one face

```text
Diameters first. Twenty-four, then forty, then thirty. [pause]
Now the lengths. Take them all from the left-hand face. [pause]
That face is the datum. Everything is measured from it. [pause]
If you chain the lengths instead, every small error adds to the next one. [pause]
From one datum, each length is wrong on its own only. That is why we do it.
```

## Compression springs

_Topic id `compression-springs` · 5 steps · folder `public/sounds/technical-drawing/compression-springs/`_

#### `compression-springs/spring-idea.mp3` — Nobody draws a real helix

```text
A spring is a helix. A helix is a curve going round and along at the same time. [pause]
Drawing that curve properly takes an hour and nobody does it. [pause]
So the standard says: draw the coils as straight sloping lines. [pause]
Everyone reads it as a spring. That is a convention doing its job. [pause]
A compression spring is pushed. It gets shorter under load.
```

#### `compression-springs/spring-envelope.mp3` — Set out the envelope

```text
First the box the spring lives in. [pause]
Centre line down the middle. [pause]
Two lines each side for the outside diameter. [pause]
Top and bottom lines for the free length — the length with no load on it. [pause]
Mean diameter is the middle of the wire. Outside is mean plus one wire.
```

#### `compression-springs/spring-coils.mp3` — Slope the coils in

```text
Now the coils, one pitch apart. [pause]
The front of each coil slopes down from left to right. [pause]
The back of the same coil comes back the other way. [pause]
Front, back, front, back. Six coils here. [pause]
Keep every line the same slope. A spring with a wandering pitch looks broken.
```

#### `compression-springs/spring-ends.mp3` — Closed and ground ends

```text
Look at the top and bottom coil. They lie flat. [pause]
That is called closed and ground. [pause]
Closed means the last coil touches the one below it. [pause]
Ground means it has been flattened on a wheel so it sits square. [pause]
Without that the spring leans over when you press it. It must sit flat.
```

#### `compression-springs/spring-dims.mp3` — The four sizes

```text
Free length one hundred and eight. [pause]
Outside diameter thirty-nine. Wire diameter five. [pause]
And six coils — write that on as a note, you cannot dimension a count. [pause]
Those four sizes let anybody wind the same spring again.
```


---

## Tension springs

_Topic id `tension-springs` · 4 steps · folder `public/sounds/technical-drawing/tension-springs/`_

#### `tension-springs/tension-idea.mp3` — Pulled, not pushed

```text
A tension spring is pulled. A compression spring is pushed. [pause]
That one difference changes the whole drawing. [pause]
A pushed spring needs gaps between the coils, so it has somewhere to go. [pause]
A pulled spring needs none. Its coils touch when it is at rest. [pause]
And it needs something to pull on. That is the loop at each end.
```

#### `tension-springs/tension-coils.mp3` — Close the coils up

```text
Same sloping lines as before, but no gaps. [pause]
The pitch is the wire diameter. Four wire, four pitch. [pause]
Fourteen coils, all touching. [pause]
It should look tight, like a coil of wire, not like a slinky.
```

#### `tension-springs/tension-loops.mp3` — The loops carry the load

```text
The last coil is turned up to make a loop. [pause]
Swing it with the compass so it is a true half circle. [pause]
One at each end, both in the same plane. [pause]
The loop is where the load goes in — and where the spring breaks first.
```

#### `tension-springs/tension-dims.mp3` — Length over the loops

```text
Careful with the length on this one. [pause]
The free length of a tension spring is measured over the loops. [pause]
Not over the coils. Over the loops, outside to outside. [pause]
Then outside diameter, wire diameter and the number of coils, same as before.
```

## Splined shafts (external)

_Topic id `splined-shaft-external` · 5 steps · folder `public/sounds/technical-drawing/splined-shaft-external/`_

#### `splined-shaft-external/spline-what.mp3` — A spline is many keys

```text
You already know the key and the keyway. [pause]
A spline is the same idea, but many keys, cut into the shaft itself. [pause]
Six of them, evenly round the shaft. [pause]
Six teeth share the drive, so each one works less and nothing shears off. [pause]
And the hub can still slide along, which is exactly what a gearbox needs.
```

#### `splined-shaft-external/spline-circles.mp3` — Two circles first

```text
Start the end view with two circles. [pause]
The big one is the major diameter — the tips of the splines. [pause]
The small one is the minor diameter — the root, the bottom of the spaces. [pause]
Sixty and fifty-four. The splines stand three millimetres proud.
```

#### `splined-shaft-external/spline-teeth.mp3` — Straight-sided teeth

```text
Now the teeth. Six of them, sixty degrees apart. [pause]
Here is the part people get wrong. [pause]
The sides of the tooth are parallel to each other. [pause]
They do not point at the centre. They are straight-sided. [pause]
Each tooth stands on the root circle and is capped by the major circle.
```

#### `splined-shaft-external/spline-side.mp3` — The side view is easy

```text
Along the shaft you do not draw all six splines. Nobody does. [pause]
Thick line for the tips, top and bottom. [pause]
Thin line just inside it for the roots. [pause]
That is the whole convention. Two thick, two thin, and the end view tells the rest.
```

#### `splined-shaft-external/spline-dims.mp3` — Call it out properly

```text
You cannot dimension six teeth one at a time. Use a note. [pause]
Six splines. Major diameter sixty. Minor fifty-four. Width fifteen. [pause]
Written once, under the view. That is how the standard wants it.
```

## What is not in this file

20 of the 45 topics in the studio are wired for voice; 25 still to write.
This file lists only the ones being recorded now — see `IN_DOC` in `scripts/build_drawing_scripts.mts`.
The rest stay wired and keep playing; their scripts are in the git history of this file.

To take the next topic on, add its id to `SCRIPTED` and `IN_DOC` and run the script again.
The clip path is always `/sounds/technical-drawing/<topic id>/<step id>.mp3`, built from those two ids in
`narrationSrc()`, so nothing has to be registered anywhere else.
